title: The Macroeconomic Policy Outlook: Q3 2026
gist: UK output per hour, measured on HMRC administrative tax data rather than the distorted Labour Force Survey, grew 1.1% a year over the two years to Q2 2026 — a genuine, broad-based (12 of 19 sectors) productivity revival that the Resolution Foundation cannot attribute to sector reallocation, low-paid job shedding, or capital deepening, leaving unexplained TFP growth (and only tentatively AI) as the likely driver.

insights.claim: UK output per hour grew 1.1% a year over the two years to Q2 2026 on administrative tax data, reversing a 0.7% annual fall in the prior two years and beating the 0.7% growth of the late 2010s (2016-2019).
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: A genuine UK productivity turnaround, if sustained, reprices long-run GDP, gilt, and sterling assumptions that were anchored to near-zero productivity.
insights.quote: Administrative tax data suggests that output per hour grew by 1.1 per cent a year over the two years to Q2 2026 – not just a sharp turnaround from the 0.7 per cent a year fall in the two years before, but also faster than the 0.7 per cent growth rate seen in the late 2010s.
insights.locator: On the whole, the 2020s has been a disastrous decade

insights.claim: The headline Labour Force Survey shows UK productivity still falling (-0.2% a year over the two years to Q2 2026), while the two more reliable measures — Resolution Foundation admin-based estimates and ONS Workforce Jobs — both show +1.1% a year, a divergence driven entirely by how much labour input is counted, not by output.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Investors relying on the ONS headline productivity print are reading a distorted signal; the admin data flips the direction of travel.
insights.quote: The LFS has muddied the waters, showing productivity growth of −0.2 per cent a year over the past two years. But the two more reliable measures both point clearly the other way, at 1.1 per cent a year on Workforce Jobs and our admin-based estimate.
insights.locator: When measured properly, annual growth in output per hour

insights.claim: The Resolution Foundation built an alternative UK employment series from HMRC PAYE Real Time Information plus self-assessment returns because RTI is a near-census immune to the falling survey response rates that distorted the LFS.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Admin-data productivity/employment series are the more trustworthy read for UK macro calls than survey-based headlines.
insights.quote: Because RTI is a near-census rather than a survey, it isn’t affected by the falling response rates that have distorted the LFS.
insights.locator: In response, the Resolution Foundation has created an alternative series

insights.claim: In 2025 the LFS recorded UK employment growth of 1.7% while HMRC admin data recorded a 0.1% fall — an implausible gap the author attributes to survey improvements rather than real hiring, and since May 2026 the ONS has advised users to focus on its administrative-data estimates.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: UK labour-market strength inferred from LFS employment growth is likely overstated; the admin read points to a flat-to-cooling jobs market.
insights.quote: In 2025, the LFS recorded employment growth of 1.7 per cent while the admin data recorded a fall of 0.1 per cent – an implausible gap that is more likely to reflect survey improvements rather than genuine employment growth.
insights.locator: Both measures use the same output series from the National Accounts

insights.claim: After the OBR cut its medium-term UK productivity assumption to around 1%, its outlook is now broadly in line with the admin-measured 1.1% reality — the author says for arguably the first time ever.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The OBR's fiscal headroom math may finally rest on a realistic productivity path, reducing the risk of forced downgrade-driven fiscal tightening.
insights.quote: after the OBR revised downward its medium-term assumption for UK productivity growth to around 1 per cent, its outlook is now in line with reality for arguably the first time ever.
insights.locator: Notably, after the OBR revised downward

insights.claim: Despite the pickup, UK output per hour in Q2 2026 was about 5% below the level implied by the OBR's final pre-Covid forecast, a lost-output gap of roughly £150 billion a year or £4,500 per worker.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The revival is a change in direction, not a recovery of the level — the UK productivity shortfall remains a large structural drag on living standards.
insights.quote: the ONS’s headline measure of output per hour worked was around 5 per cent lower than the level implied by the OBR’s final pre-Covid forecast – equating to lost output of around £150 billion a year, or around £4,500 a year per worker.
insights.locator: In Q2 2026, the ONS’s headline measure

insights.claim: Over the two years to Q2 2026 UK GDP grew 1.3% a year while hours worked were essentially flat at 0.2%, and 77% of the productivity pickup versus the prior two years came from slower hours growth rather than faster output.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The productivity gain is arithmetically a labour-input story — watch whether hours stay flat or output actually accelerates to confirm durability.
insights.quote: Three-quarters (77 per cent) of the pickup in productivity growth between those two periods comes from slower hours growth.
insights.locator: In an accounting sense, stronger productivity growth

insights.claim: Unlike the hyper-flexible US labour market where productivity growth is negatively correlated with the cycle, UK productivity growth from 1972-2019 was positively correlated with employment growth and only slightly negatively correlated with hours growth.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Standard US-style cyclical intuition (weak jobs = strong productivity) misfires for the UK, so this pickup is harder to dismiss as a routine downturn artefact.
insights.quote: In the US – with its hyper-flexible labour market – these channels mean that productivity growth is negatively correlated with the labour market cycle... But the UK is not the US: between 1972 and 2019, UK productivity growth was positively correlated with employment growth
insights.locator: One might think that a productivity rebound is inevitable

insights.claim: The historic UK correlation implies the 1.4pp slowdown in hours growth should have lifted productivity growth by only 0.3pp — explaining just a sixth of the 1.9pp improvement actually observed.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Roughly five-sixths of the UK productivity pickup is beyond what the labour-market cycle can account for, pointing to a real underlying gain.
insights.quote: the 1.4 percentage point slowdown in hours growth... would be expected to raise productivity growth by just 0.3 percentage points – explaining only a sixth of 1.9 percentage point improvement that we have seen.
insights.locator: Given this historic correlation

themes.theme: Ruling out sector reallocation and job shedding

insights.claim: Almost all of the UK productivity pickup came from faster growth within sectors, not from reallocating hours between them; a decomposition of 19 industries shows the reallocation term is a rounding error against a 1.1pp within-industry contribution.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The gain is genuine within-firm efficiency, not a statistical mix-shift — a more investable and potentially durable form of growth.
insights.quote: Compared to an average within-industry contribution of 1.1 percentage points over the past two years, the reallocation term is a rounding error.
insights.locator: Figure 3 decomposes four-quarter growth

insights.claim: The share of UK employees in hospitality was 6.6% in Q2 2026, identical to its 2016-2019 share and only 0.3pp below its Q4 2022 post-Covid peak, contradicting the claim that higher employment costs shrank the sector to flatter aggregate productivity.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Narratives blaming NICs and minimum-wage rises for gutting low-pay sectors are not borne out in the employment-share data.
insights.quote: Hospitality... accounted for 6.6 per cent of employee jobs in Q2 2026, the same share as in 2016-2019 and just 0.3 percentage points below its peak in the immediate post-Covid rebound (6.9 per cent in Q4 2022).
insights.locator: At this level of aggregation at least

insights.claim: The April 2025 UK increases to employer NICs, the National Living Wage and minimum wage raised the cost of employing a part-time minimum-wage worker by 14%, which the Resolution Foundation estimates could cost around 80,000 jobs — just 0.2% of total employment.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The much-debated 2025 employment-cost hike is too small to explain the productivity move and only a marginal drag on aggregate jobs.
insights.quote: Our own analysis put the combined effect of these policies at a 14 per cent rise in the cost of employing a part-time minimum-wage worker, which could result in around 80,000 fewer jobs.
insights.locator: The policies in question are the April 2025 increases

insights.claim: Across ~400 UK occupations, jobs paying below the 2024 median grew 3.4% in the year to April 2025 versus 1.4% for above-median jobs — a 2pp gap favouring lower-paid roles, the opposite of the low-pay shakeout narrative.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Low-paid work was not being shed as costs rose, so the productivity gain is not a composition trick — it is broad and worker-general.
insights.quote: The number of jobs grew by 3.4 per cent in occupations paying below the median in 2024, against 1.4 per cent in those paying above it – a gap of 2 percentage points in favour of lower-paid occupations.
insights.locator: Take the year to April 2025

insights.claim: Essentially all of the UK's 2.3% real pay growth in the year to April 2025 came from higher pay within occupations, with the shifting occupational mix contributing -0.1pp versus a +0.7pp average over the preceding three years.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Real wage gains are being driven by genuine within-job productivity, supportive of sustained consumer spending power if it holds.
insights.quote: Essentially all the 2.3 per cent real pay growth in 2025 came from higher pay within occupations rather than from a change in the mix of occupations.
insights.locator: Figure 5 shows what the broader composition

insights.claim: The UK productivity pickup is broad: 12 of 19 sectors made a positive contribution over the past two years and 12 contributed more than in the prior two years, so it is not one sector flattering the aggregate.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Breadth makes the revival harder to dismiss as noise and points to an economy-wide rather than sector-specific driver.
insights.quote: The improvement is broad: 12 of the 19 sectors made a positive contribution over the past two years, and 12 contributed more than they did in the two years before.
insights.locator: Figure 4 shows each sector’s average contribution

insights.claim: Information and communication is the single largest contributor at 0.5pp a year with Q2 2026 sector output up 2.7% led by computer programming, but ICT already added 0.4pp a year in 2016-2019 before commercial AI existed, so its strength should not be read as purely an AI effect.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Attributing the UK's ICT-led productivity gain to AI is premature — the sector was a bright spot long before AI, cautioning against an AI-priced UK growth trade.
insights.quote: The sector contributed 0.4 percentage points a year to aggregate productivity growth in 2016-2019, well before AI existed in any commercial form. Therefore, it is worth resisting the temptation to read its recent strength as purely an AI effect.
insights.locator: Information and communication (ICT) is the largest single contributor

insights.claim: UK financial and insurance output fell 8.3% over 2023-2024 and remains 9.8% below its 2016-2019 average, so its swing from -0.7 to +0.01pp productivity contribution reflects a sector that has stopped shrinking rather than genuinely growing.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Part of the services-led rebound is base-effect recovery from acute weakness, not a boom — tempering how bullish to be on the trajectory.
insights.quote: Financial and insurance output fell by 8.3 per cent over 2023 and 2024, before growing 0.2 per cent in 2025, leaving it 9.8 per cent below its 2016-2019 average. It has stopped shrinking rather than truly growing.
insights.locator: Some of this reflects a recovery from a period of acute weakness

insights.claim: The wholesale and retail sector's productivity contribution rose from -0.2 to +0.2pp and hospitality's from -0.2pp to zero, meaning the two sectors most blamed for flattering figures via layoffs instead helped drive the pickup by becoming more productive.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Low-pay service sectors are contributing real productivity gains, reinforcing that the revival is genuine and worker-general.
insights.quote: the two sectors most often blamed for flattering the figures by laying off workers, have instead helped drive the pickup by becoming more productive.
insights.locator: Instead, it is services that are driving the pickup

insights.claim: UK total gross fixed capital formation was flat at 19% of GDP in both 2023 and 2025, and with investment stalled the author rules out capital deepening as the cause of the productivity rebound.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The gain is not bought with capex, so it cannot be sustained by simply extrapolating an investment boom that has not occurred.
insights.quote: total gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) was 19 per cent of GDP in both 2023 and 2025... For capital deepening to explain a pickup in productivity growth, a sharp uptick in the level of investment is needed.
insights.locator: Looking beyond public investment alone

insights.claim: As UK investment rose 2 percentage points of GDP between 2010 and 2016, capital deepening swung from a 0.4pp drag to a 1.0pp boost on market-sector productivity — showing sustained higher investment is what historically moves productivity, and it has been absent recently.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the scale of investment rise (2pp of GDP) needed to lift UK productivity through capital, a level policymakers have not delivered this cycle.
insights.quote: Between 2010 and 2016, investment rose by 2 percentage points of GDP, and capital deepening went from a 0.4 percentage point drag on productivity growth to a 1.0 percentage point boost.
insights.locator: This happened in the mid-2010s

insights.claim: Labour's public sector net investment is 2.7% of GDP in 2025-26, only marginally above the 2.4% and 2.6% of the prior two years, so Chancellor Rachel Reeves cancelling planned cuts spared a future drag rather than raising current growth.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The current productivity pickup cannot be credited to fiscal investment policy, which is roughly flat versus the previous government's plans.
insights.quote: Labour’s plans set public sector net investment at 2.7 per cent of GDP in 2025-26, only marginally above its level in the previous two years... such a marginal uplift in public investment cannot explain the size of the productivity rebound.
insights.locator: But that only spared Britain a future drag

themes.theme: TFP mystery and the AI question

insights.claim: With reallocation and capital deepening ruled out, the UK productivity gain looks like total factor productivity growth — the growth-accounting residual that all but vanished after the financial crisis and that Abramovitz called a measure of our ignorance about the causes of growth.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The revival's driver is genuinely unexplained, so its persistence is uncertain — an upside optionality on UK growth that cannot yet be underwritten.
insights.quote: we are left with what looks like one of the most mysterious quantities in economics: total factor productivity (TFP) growth.
insights.locator: With reallocation and capital deepening ruled out

insights.claim: The share of UK businesses (excluding sub-10-employee micro-SMEs) using AI doubled from 23% in Sept-Oct 2023 to 46% in June 2026, but only 9.9% of AI-using firms — around 4.6% of all businesses — use it extensively.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: AI adoption is wide but shallow, so it is likely too early for AI to be the mechanical cause of the measured productivity revival.
insights.quote: the proportion of UK businesses using AI has doubled in the past three years, from 23 per cent in September-October 2023 to 46 per cent in June 2026. But only one-in-ten (9.9 per cent) of these AI-using businesses – or around one-in-twenty (4.6 per cent) of all businesses – are currently using it extensively.
insights.locator: It’s true that the prevalence of AI use has expanded rapidly

insights.claim: UK firms are far more optimistic about AI's future than its record so far: 62% expect a positive impact on revenue per employee over the next three years versus only 17% who say it has had a positive impact over the past three years.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: The realized AI productivity dividend is still small; a large gap between expectation and delivered impact frames the risk in AI-driven growth forecasts.
insights.quote: Three-fifths (62 per cent) say it will have a positive impact on revenue per employee in the next three years, versus less than a fifth (17 per cent) who say it has had a positive impact over the past three years.
insights.locator: UK businesses are certainly positive about the future impact

insights.claim: The author frames an unexplained UK productivity improvement as a far better problem than the unexplained decline after the financial crisis, because it is real and broad — workers across the economy are producing more rather than the least productive parts simply shrinking.
insights.speaker: Stephen Hunsaker
insights.so_what: Sets a constructive read on the UK growth backdrop, but the lack of an identified driver is the key risk to extrapolating it.
insights.quote: an unexplained improvement is a far better problem to have than the unexplained decline that followed the financial crisis.
insights.locator: For now, the revival of productivity growth looks as mysterious as its fall
